claim: VOTC reliably encodes sound categories in sighted and early blind individuals using a representational structure and connectivity partially similar to the one found in vision.
source: We used fMRI to characterize VOTC responses to eight categories presented acoustically in sighted and early blind individuals, and visually in a separate sighted group. We observed that VOTC reliably encodes sound categories in sighted and blind people using a representational structure and connectivity partially similar to the one found in vision.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including topographical maps, decoding analyses, and representational similarity analyses.

claim: Sound categories are more reliably encoded in the blind than the sighted group.
source: Sound categories were, however, more reliably encoded in the blind than the sighted group, using a representational format closer to the one found in vision.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding accuracy data and inter-subject correlation analyses presented in the results section.

claim: VOTC in blind represents the categorical membership of sounds rather than their acoustic features.
source: Crucially, VOTC in blind represents the categorical membership of sounds rather than their acoustic features.
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis comparing brain dissimilarity matrices with behavioral and acoustic models.

claim: The occipital cortex of blind individuals massively extends its response repertoire to non-visual inputs.
source: One of the most striking demonstrations of experience-dependent plasticity comes from studies of blind individuals showing that the occipital cortex (traditionally considered as visual) massively extends its response repertoire to non-visual inputs (Neville and Bavelier, 2002; Sadato et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The functional organization of occipital regions develops based on innate protomaps implementing computational bias for low-level visual features.
source: In fact, the functional organization of occipital regions has been thought to develop based on innate protomaps implementing a computational bias for low-level visual features including ﻿retinal eccentricity bias (Malach et al., 2002), orientation content (Rice et al., 2014), spatial frequency content (Rajimehr et al., 2011) and ﻿the average curvilinearity/rectilinearity of stimuli (Nasr et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: In absence of visual experience, the functional organization of the occipital cortex could not develop according to visual proto-organization and may switch functional tuning toward distant computations.
source: Consequently, in absence of visual experience, the functional organization of the occipital cortex could not develop according to this visual proto-organization and those regions may therefore switch their functional tuning toward distant computations (Bedny, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous theoretical work and represents a hypothesis being tested in the current study.

claim: The occipital cortex of congenitally blind people maintains a division of computational labor similar to the one characterizing the sighted brain.
source: In striking contrast with this view, several studies suggested that the occipital cortex of congenitally blind people maintains a division of computational labor somewhat similar to the one characterizing the sighted brain (Amedi et al., 2010; Dormal and Collignon, 2011; Ricciardi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: VOTC shows a medial to lateral segregation in response to living and non-living visual stimuli in sighted individuals.
source: In sighted individuals, lesion and neuroimaging studies have demonstrated that VOTC shows a medial to lateral segregation in response to living and non-living visual stimuli, respectively, and that some specific regions respond preferentially to visual objects of specific categories like the fusiform face area (FFA; Kanwisher et al., 1997; Tong et al., 2000), the extrastriate body area (EBA; Downing et al., 2001) or the parahippocampal place area (PPA; Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous lesion and neuroimaging studies.

claim: In early blind people, the functional preference for various categories partially overlaps with similar categorical responses in sighted people when processing visual inputs.
source: Interestingly, In early blind people, the functional preference for words (Reich et al., 2011) or letters (Striem-Amit et al., 2012), motion (Dormal et al., 2016; Poirier et al., 2004), places (He et al., 2013; Wolbers et al., 2011), bodies (Kitada et al., 2014; Striem-Amit and Amedi, 2014), tools (Peelen et al., 2013) and shapes (Amedi et al., 2007) partially overlaps with similar categorical responses in sighted people when processing visual inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: The large-scale categorical layout in VOTC shares similarities between sighted and blind people.
source: Distributed multivariate pattern analyses (Haxby et al., 2001) have also supported the idea that the large-scale categorical layout in VOTC shares similarities between sighted and blind people (Handjaras et al., 2016; van den Hurk et al., 2017; Peelen et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous multivariate pattern analysis studies.

claim: The response patterns elicited by sounds of four different categories in the VOTC of blind people could successfully predict the categorical response to images of the same categories in the VOTC of sighted controls.
source: A recent study demonstrated that the response patterns elicited by sounds of four different categories in the VOTC of blind people could successfully predict the categorical response to images of the same categories in the VOTC of sighted controls, suggesting overlapping distributed categorical responses in sighted for vision and in blind for sounds (van den Hurk et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The occipital cortex of blind people may represent acoustic features which form the basis of categorical selectivity in the auditory cortex.
source: Indeed, several studies involving congenitally blind have shown that their occipital cortex may represent acoustic features – for instance frequencies (Huber et al., 2019; Watkins et al., 2013) – which form the basis of the development of categorical selectivity in the auditory cortex (Moerel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Not all regions in VOTC are affected to the same extent by crossmodal plasticity reorganization.
source: Moreover, the degree of similarity between the categorical representation in sighted and in blind might differ across different categories: not all the regions in VOTC seem to be affected to the same extent by the crossmodal plasticity reorganization (Bi et al., 2016; Dormal et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The auditory selectivity maps of the blind subjects partially matched the visual map obtained in sighted controls during vision (r = 0.19, pFDR <0.001).
source: The auditory selectivity maps of the blind subjects partially matched the visual map obtained in sighted controls during vision (r = 0.19, pFDR <0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of topographical selectivity maps shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A similar selectivity map was observed in the sighted controls using sounds, with significant correlation both with visual map in sighted (r = 0.14, pFDR <0.001), and with the auditory map in blinds (r = 0.06, pFDR = 0.001).
source: In addition, a similar selectivity map was also observed in the sighted controls using sounds. The correlation was significant both with visual map in sighted (r = 0.14, pFDR <0.001), and with the auditory map in blinds (r = 0.06, pFDR = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of topographical selectivity maps shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The correlation between EBa and SCa was significantly lower than both the correlation between SCv and EBa (pFDR. = 0.0003) and the correlation between SCv and SCa (pFDR = 0.0004).
source: The correlation between EBa and SCa was significantly lower than both the correlation between SCv and EBa (pFDR. = 0.0003) and the correlation between SCv and SCa (pFDR = 0.0004).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of correlation values from topographical selectivity maps.

claim: The magnitude of correlation between EBa and SCv was not significantly different from the correlation between SCa and SCv (pFDR = 0.233).
source: Instead, the magnitude of correlation between EBa and SCv was not significantly different from the correlation between SCa and SCv (pFDR = 0.233).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of correlation values from topographical selectivity maps.

claim: The Jaccard similarity was significant in each category and in each group (in all cases p<0.001, after FDR correction).
source: The one sample T-test revealed a significant Jaccard similarity in each category and in each group (in all cases p<0.001, after FDR correction for the 12 comparisons: three groups * four categories), highlighting a significant consistency of the topographical maps for each category between subjects belonging to the same group.
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-tests on Jaccard similarity indices.

claim: There was a significant main effect of Category (F(3,138)=18.369; p=<0.001) and a significant interaction Group*Category (F(6,138)=4.9; p=<0.001) in the Jaccard similarity analysis.
source: We performed a repeated measures ANOVA to look at the differences between categories and groups. We obtained a significant main effect of Category (F(3,138)=18.369; p=<0.001) and a significant interaction Group*Category (F(6,138)=4.9; p=<0.001), instead the main effect of Group was not significant (F(2,46)=1.83; p.17).
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated measures ANOVA on Jaccard similarity data.

claim: In SCv, the consistency of the topographical maps for the visual stimuli was similar for each category.
source: In SCv we did not find any difference between categories, meaning that the consistency (i.e. the Jaccard similarity) of the topographical maps for the visual stimuli in sighted was similar for each category.
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc analysis of Jaccard similarity data.

claim: In the SCa group, the consistency of the topographical maps in the big object and places was significantly higher compared to the consistency in the humans and animals' categories.
source: In the SCa group, the only two significant differences emerged between the category 'big objects and places' and the two animate categories: humans (p=0.01) and animals (p<0.008). In both cases the consistency of the topographical maps in the big object and places was significantly higher compared to the consistency in the humans and animals' categories.
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc analysis of Jaccard similarity data.

claim: In the blind group, the animal category showed significantly lower Jaccard similarity compared to other categories.
source: Finally, in the blind group only the humans and the manipulable objects categories did not show a significant difference. The animal category was, indeed, significantly lower than the humans (p=0.01), the manipulable objects (p=0.008) and the big objects and places (p=0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc analysis of Jaccard similarity data.

claim: The animals' category showed a significantly lower Jaccard similarity within the EBa group compared to both SCa (p=0.008) and SCv (p=0.001) groups.
source: The animals' category showed a significantly lower Jaccard similarity within the EBa group compared to both SCa (p=0.008) and SCv (p=0.001) groups while the similarity of big objects and places category was significantly higher in EBa compared to SCv (p=0.038).
evidence: This claim is supported by between-group comparison of Jaccard similarity data.

claim: The one-sample T-tests revealed a significant similarity between EBa and SCv and between SCa and SCv in each category (pFDR <0.001 in all cases).
source: The one-sample T-tests revealed a significant similarity between EBa and SCv and between SCa and SCv in each category (pFDR <0.001 in all cases).
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-tests on Jaccard similarity indices comparing groups.

claim: The Jaccard similarity was higher between the big objects and places category compared to the other three categories (animal: p<0.001; human: p<0.001; manipulable: p<0.001).
source: The repeated measures ANOVA highlighted a significant main effect of Category (F(2.2,69.8) = 31.17, p<0.001). In both groups' comparisons the Jaccard similarity was higher between the big objects and places category compared to the other three categories (animal: p<0.001; human: p<0.001; manipulable: p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated measures ANOVA and post-hoc tests on Jaccard similarity data.

claim: In SCv, a smaller number of voxels shows selectivity for the human category compared to the others.
source: In SCv we found that a smaller number of voxels shows selectivity for the human category compared to the others (human vs animal: t(15)=-3.27; pFDR = 0.03; human vs manipulable: t(15)=2.60; pFDR = 0.08; human vs big: t(15)=-4.16; pFDR = 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of voxel counts shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In EBa, there is a lower number of voxels preferring animals compared to non-living categories.
source: In EBa, instead, there is a lower number of voxels preferring animals compare to non-living categories (animals vs manipulable: t(15)=-2.47; pFDR = 0.09; animals vs big: t(15)=-3.22; pFDR = 0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of voxel counts shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In SCa, the number of voxels selective for the big and place category was significantly higher than the number of voxels selective for the manipulable category (t(16)=3.27; pFDR = 0.03).
source: Finally, in SCa the number of voxels selective for the big and place category was significantly higher than the number of voxels selective for the manipulable category (t(16)=3.27; pFDR = 0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of voxel counts.

claim: The main difference in voxel counts between groups emerged from the animal category, with reduced number of voxels selective for animals in EBa compared to SCv (p=0.02).
source: Importantly, when we look at the difference between the 3 groups for each category, the main difference emerged from the animal category. In this category, the ANOVA revealed a main effect of group (F(2,46)=3.91; p=0.03). The post hoc comparisons revealed that this difference was mainly driven by the reduced number of voxels selective for the animal category in EBa compared to SCv (p=0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA and post-hoc analysis of voxel counts.

claim: In SCv and in EBa, the averaged decoding accuracy was significantly higher than chance level in both EVC and VOTC.
source: In SCv and in EBa the averaged decoding accuracy was significantly higher than chance level in both EVC (SCv: DA = 69%; t(15)=6.69, pFDR <0.00001; EBa: DA = 55%; t(15)=4.48, pFDR = 0.0006) and VOTC (SCv: DA = 71%; t(15)=7.37, pFDR <0.00001; EBa: DA = 57%; t(15)=8.00, pFDR <0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by binary decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the SCa, the averaged decoding accuracy was significantly higher than the chance level in VOTC but not in EVC.
source: In the SCa the averaged decoding accuracy was significantly higher than the chance level in VOTC (DA = 54%; t(16)=4.32, pFDR = 0.0006) but not in EVC (DA = 51%; t(16)=1.70, pFDR = 0.11).
evidence: This claim is supported by binary decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Independent sample t-tests revealed higher decoding accuracy values in EBa when compared to SCa in both EVC and VOTC.
source: Moreover, independent sample t-tests revealed higher decoding accuracy values in EBa when compared to SCa in both EVC (t(31)=2.52, pFDR = 0.017) and VOTC (t(31)=2.08, pFDR = 0.046).
evidence: This claim is supported by independent sample t-tests on decoding accuracy data.

claim: In EVC, the permutation test revealed a significant positive correlation only between the SCv and the EBa DSMs (mean r = 0.19; pFDR = 0.0002).
source: In EVC, the permutation test revealed a significant positive correlation only between the SCv and the EBa DSMs (mean r = 0.19; pFDR = 0.0002), whereas negative correlation emerged from the correlation between the SCv and SCa DSMs (mean r = –.18; pFDR <0.001) and the correlation between the SCa and the EBa DSMs (mean r = –0.03; pFDR = 0.18).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test on correlation between dissimilarity matrices.

claim: In VOTC, significant correlations were observed for all the groups' pairs: SCv and EBa (r = 0.34; pFDR = 0.0002), SCv and SCa (r = 0.1; pFDR = 0.002), SCa and EBa (r = 0.1; pFDR = 0.002).
source: In VOTC, we observed a significant correlation for all the groups' pairs: SCv and EBa (r = 0.34; pFDR = 0.0002), SCv and SCa (r = 0.1; pFDR = 0.002), SCa and EBa (r = 0.1; pFDR = 0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test on correlation between dissimilarity matrices.

claim: The correlation between SCv and EBa was significantly higher compared to both the correlation between SCv and SCa and the correlation between SCa and EBa in VOTC.
source: Moreover, the correlation between SCv and EBa was significantly higher compared to both the correlation between SCv and SCa (corr. diff = 0.25; pFDR = 0.008) and the correlation between SCa and EBa (corr. diff = 0.25; pFDR = 0.008).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of correlation values.

claim: In VOTC of SCv, when the hierarchical clustering was stopped at 2 clusters, there was a clear living vs non-living distinction.
source: In VOTC the most striking results are related to the way the animal category is represented in the EBa group compared to the SCv. In fact, when the hierarchical clustering was stopped at 2 clusters in SCv, we observed a clear living vs non-living distinction.
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In EBa, when clustering was stopped at 2 clusters, the division was between humans and non-humans (including all the non-living categories plus the animals).
source: In EBa, instead, the division was between humans and non-humans (including all the non-living categories plus the animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: When the clusters are 3 in SCv, there is a separation into (1) non-living; (2) human; (3) animals.
source: When the clusters are 3, we see in SCv a separation into (1) non-living; (2) human; (3) animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In EBa with 3 clusters, the animals keep being clustered with non-living, with clusters being: (1) Non-living and animals; (2) Human vocalization voices; (3) Human non-vocalization voices.
source: In EBa, instead, the animals keep in being clustered with non-living, in a way that the 3 clusters are: (1) Non-living and animals; (2) Human vocalization voices; (3) Human non-vocalization voices.
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the case of 4 clusters, in both SCv and EBa the additional 4th cluster is represented by the manipulable-tools category.
source: In the case of the 4 clusters, in both SCv and EBa the additional 4th cluster is represented by the manipulable-tools category, while in the EBa the animals remain with the rest of the non-living categories.
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The three behavioral DSMs were highly correlated (SCa/EBa: r = 0.85, p<0.001; SCa/SCv: r = 0.95, p<0.001; EBa/SCv: r = 0.89, p<0.001).
source: The three DSMs were highly correlated (SCa/EBa: r = 0.85, p<0.001; SCa/SCv: r = 0.95, p<0.001; EBa/SCv: r = 0.89, p<0.001), revealing a similar way to group the stimuli across the three groups following mostly a categorical strategy to classify the stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of behavioral dissimilarity matrices.

claim: In SCv, the EVC's DSM was significantly correlated with the Hmax-C1 model (mean r = 0.13, p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.002) but not with the behavioral model (mean r = 0.03; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.11).
source: The permutation test revealed that in SCv the EVC's DSM was significantly correlated with the Hmax-C1 model (mean r = 0.13, p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.002) but not with the behavioral model (mean r = 0.03; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.11).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In SCv, VOTC's DSM was significantly positively correlated with the behavioral model (mean r = 0.34; pFDR <0.001) but negatively correlated with the Hmax-C1 model (r = –.07; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.991.).
source: The permutation test, showed that VOTC's DSM, instead, was significantly positively correlated with the behavioral model (mean r = 0.34; pFDR <0.001) but negative correlated with the Hmax-C1 model (r = –.07; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.991.).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the EBa and SCa groups, EVC's DSMs were not significantly correlated with neither the behavioral nor the pitch model.
source: In the EBa and SCa groups, EVC's DSMs were not significantly correlated with neither the behavioral (EBa: mean r = 0.004; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.47; SCa: mean r = –0.11, p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.98) nor the pitch model (EBa: mean r = –0.08; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.94; SCa: mean r = –0.09, p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.98).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The VOTC's DSMs were significantly correlated with the behavioral model in EBa (mean r = 0.12, p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.02) but not in SCa (mean r = 0.06; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.17).
source: In contrast, the VOTC's DSMs were significantly correlated with the behavioral model in EBa (mean r = 0.12, p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.02) but not in SCa (mean r = 0.06; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.17).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The VOTC's DSMs were not significantly correlated with the pitch model neither in EBa nor in SCa.
source: Finally the VOTC's DSMs were not significantly correlated with the pitch model neither in EBa(mean r = –0.03; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.49), nor in SCa(mean r = 0.03; p(one-tailed)FDR = 0.39);
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis.

claim: A 2 Groups (EBa/SCa) X 2 Models (behavioral/pitch) ANOVA in VOTC revealed a significant main effect of Model (F(1,31)=11.37, p=0.002) and a significant interaction Group X Model (F(1,31)=4.03, p=0.05).
source: In addition, a 2 Groups (EBa/SCa) X 2 Models (behavioral/pitch) ANOVA in VOTC revealed a significant main effect of Model (F(1,31)=11.37, p=0.002) and a significant interaction Group X Model (F(1,31)=4.03, p=0.05), whereas the main effect of Group (F(1,31)=2.38−4, p=0.98), was non-significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA on representational similarity analysis data.

claim: The correlation between subjects' DSMs in the within group condition was significant in SCv (r = 0.42; pFDR <0.001) and EBa (r = 0.10; pFDR <0.001), but not in SCa (r = –.03; pFDR = 0.98).
source: The permutation test revealed that the correlation between subjects' DSMs in the within group condition was significant in SCv (r = 0.42; pFDR <0.001) and EBa (r = 0.10; pFDR <0.001), whereas it was not significant in SCa (r = –.03; pFDR = 0.98).
evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The correlation between subjects' DSMs was significant in all the three between groups conditions (SCv-EBa: r = 0.17, pFDR <0.001; SCv-SCa: r = 0.04, pFDR = 0.002; EBa-SCa: r = 0.02; pFDR = 0.04).
source: Moreover, the correlation between subjects' DSMs was significant in all the three between groups conditions (SCv-EBa: r = 0.17, pFDR <0.001; SCv-SCa: r = 0.04, pFDR = 0.002; EBa-SCa: r = 0.02; pFDR = 0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The highest inter-subject correlation is the within SCv group condition, which was significantly higher compared to all the other five conditions.
source: When we ranked the correlations values (Figure 7) we observed that the highest inter-subject correlation is the within SCv group condition, which was significantly higher compared to all the other five conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Both the between groups SCv-EBa and the within group EBa correlations were significantly higher compared to the last 3 inter-subjects correlation's values (between SCv-SCa; between EBa-SCa; within SCa).
source: Interestingly, both the between groups SCv-EBa and the within group EBa correlations were significantly higher compared to the last 3 inter-subjects correlation's values (between SCv-SCa; between EBa-SCa; within SCa).
evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The representational connectivity profile of VOTC with the rest of the brain is significantly correlated between all pairs of groups (SCv-EBa: mean r = 0.18, pFDR = 0.001; SCv-SCa: mean r = 0.14, pFDR <0.001; EBa-SCa: mean r = 0.16, pFDR <0.001).
source: The permutation analysis highlighted that the representational connectivity profile of VOTC with the rest of the brain is significantly correlated between all pairs of groups (SCv-EBa: mean r = 0.18, pFDR = 0.001; SCv-SCa: mean r = 0.14, pFDR <0.001; EBa-SCa: mean r = 0.16, pFDR <0.001), and with no difference between groups' pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by representational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: In EVC, the permutation analysis revealed a significant correlation only between the representational connectivity profile of the two groups of sighted: SCv and SCa (mean r = 0.17, pFDR <0.001).
source: In this case the permutation analysis revealed a significant correlation only between the representational connectivity profile of the two groups of sighted: SCv and SCa (mean r = 0.17, pFDR <0.001), whereas the correlation between the EBa was not significant neither with SCv (mean r = 0.06, pFDR = 0.12) nor with SCa (mean r = 0.06, pFDR = 0.11).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational connectivity analysis in EVC.

claim: VOTC shows categorical responses to sounds in the sighted and the blind in a representational format partially similar to the one elicited by images of the same categories in sighted people.
source: Our study goes beyond previous results in at least six significant ways. First, our results demonstrate that VOTC shows categorical responses to sounds in the sighted and the blind in a representational format partially similar to the one elicited by images of the same categories in sighted people (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple analyses including topographical maps and decoding analyses.

claim: Blind people show higher decoding accuracies and higher inter-subject consistency in the representation of auditory categories.
source: Second, we observed that blind people show higher decoding accuracies and higher inter-subject consistency in the representation of auditory categories, and that the representational structure of visual categories in sighted was significantly closer to the structure of the auditory categories in blind than in sighted group (see Figure 1B, Figure 3, Figure 4B, Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding accuracy and inter-subject correlation analyses.

claim: In absence of feed-forward visual input, VOTC increases its intrinsic representation of non-visual information.
source: This points to the idea that in absence of feed-forward visual input, VOTC increases its intrinsic representation of non-visual information.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of higher decoding accuracies in blind compared to sighted for auditory categories.

claim: VOTC shows similar large-scale representational connectivity profiles when processing images in sighted and sounds in sighted and blind people.
source: Third, VOTC shows similar large-scale representational connectivity profiles when processing images in sighted and sounds in sighted and blind people (see Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational connectivity analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The functional tuning of a region is determined by large-scale connectivity patterns with regions involved in similar coding strategies.
source: This result provides strong support to the general hypothesis that the functional tuning of a region is determined by large-scale connectivity patterns with regions involved in similar coding strategies (Behrens and Sporns, 2012; Mahon and Caramazza, 2011; Passingham et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work and by the representational connectivity results.

claim: Categorical membership is the main factor that predicts the representational structure of sounds in VOTC in blind people, rather than lower-level acoustical attributes of sounds.
source: By harnessing the opportunities provided by representational similarity analysis, we demonstrate that categorical membership is the main factor that predicts the representational structure of sounds in VOTC in blind people (see Figure 6), rather than lower-level acoustical attributes of sounds that are at least partially at the basis of category selectivity in the temporal cortex (Moerel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis comparing brain DSMs with behavioral and acoustic models.

claim: The between-groups Jaccard similarity analysis revealed a domain–by–modality interaction, with the big objects and places category showing a higher degree of similarity between the auditory and visual representations compared to the other categories.
source: Fifth, we provided a qualitative exploration of the structure of the categorical representation in the VOTC. The between-groups Jaccard similarity analysis revealed a domain–by–modality interaction (see Figure 2C), with the big objects and places category showing an higher degree of similarity between the auditory and visual representations compared to the other categories.
evidence: This claim is supported by Jaccard similarity analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both the hierarchical clustering and the within-group Jaccard similarity analysis highlighted a domain-by-sensory experience interaction, with the animal category represented differently in blind compared to sighted subjects.
source: In addition, both, the hierarchical clustering and the within-group Jaccard similarity analysis highlighted a domain-by-sensory experience interaction (see Figure 5 and Figure 2B), with the animal category represented differently in blind compared to sighted subjects (Bi et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering and Jaccard similarity analyses.

claim: Categorical membership is encoded in the EVC of blind people only, using a representational format that does not relate neither to the acoustic nor to the categorical structure of the stimuli.
source: Finally, our study discloses that categorical membership is encoded in the EVC of blind people only, using a representational format that does not relate neither to the acoustic nor to the categorical structure of our stimuli, suggesting different mechanisms of reorganization in this posterior occipital region.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding and representational similarity analyses in EVC.

claim: Regular visual properties specific to each category like retinotopic eccentricity biases, curvature or spatial frequencies could drive the development of categorical response in VOTC for visual information.
source: It was suggested that regular visual properties specific to each category like retinotopic eccentricity biases (Gomez et al., 2019; Malach et al., 2002), curvature (Nasr et al., 2014) or spatial frequencies (Rajimehr et al., 2011) could drive the development of categorical response in VOTC for visual information (Andrews et al., 2010; Baldassi et al., 2013; Bracci et al., 2018; Rice et al., 2014; see Op de Beeck et al., 2019 for a recent review on the emergence of category selectivity in VOTC).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The parahippocampal place area (PPA) and the fusiform face area (FFA) receive dominant inputs from downstream regions of the visual system with differential selectivity for high vs low spatial frequencies and peripheral vs. foveal inputs, causing them to respond differentially to place and face stimuli.
source: For instance, the parahippocampal place area (PPA) and the fusiform face area (FFA) receive dominant inputs from downstream regions of the visual system with differential selectivity for high vs low spatial frequencies and peripheral vs. foveal inputs, causing them to respond differentially to place and face stimuli (Levy et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A proto-eccentricity map is evident early in development.
source: For instance, a proto-eccentricity map is evident early in development (Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017) and monkeys trained early in life to discriminate different categories varying in their curvilinearity/rectilinearity develop distinct and consistent functional clusters for these categories (Srihasam et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Adults who had intensive visual experience with Pokémon early in life demonstrate distinct distributed cortical responses to this trained visual category with a systematic location supposed to be based on retinal eccentricity.
source: Further, adults who had intensive visual experience with Pokémon early in life demonstrate distinct distributed cortical responses to this trained visual category with a systematic location supposed to be based on retinal eccentricity (Gomez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Category membership independently of visual attributes is a key developmental factor that determines the consistent functional topography of the VOTC.
source: Although our results by no means disprove the observations that inherent visual biases can influence the development of the functional topography of high-level vision (Gomez et al., 2019; Hasson et al., 2002; Nasr et al., 2014), our data however suggest that category membership independently of visual attributes is also a key developmental factor that determines the consistent functional topography of the VOTC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing categorical responses in VOTC for sounds in blind and sighted.

claim: VOTC responds to sounds using a similar distributed functional profile to the one found in response to vision, even in case of people that have never had visual experience.
source: Our study demonstrates that VOTC responds to sounds using a similar distributed functional profile to the one found in response to vision, even in case of people that have never had visual experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data comparing blind and sighted groups.

claim: Previous studies reported a residual categorical effect in VOTC when orthogonalizing category membership and visual features of visual stimuli.
source: By orthogonalizing category membership and visual features of visual stimuli, previous studies reported a residual categorical effect in VOTC, highlighting how some of the variance in the neural data of VOTC might be explained by high-level categorical properties of the stimuli even when the contribution of the basic low-level features has been controlled for (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016; Kaiser et al., 2016; Proklova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Category-selectivity has been observed in VOTC during semantic tasks when word stimuli were used.
source: Category-selectivity has also been observed in VOTC during semantic tasks when word stimuli were used, suggesting an involvement of the occipito-temporal cortex in the retrieval of category-specific conceptual information (Handjaras et al., 2016; Borghesani et al., 2016; Peelen and Downing, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Learning to associate semantic features and spatial contextual associations with novel objects influences VOTC representations.
source: Moreover, previous research has shown that learning to associate semantic features (e.g., 'floats') and spatial contextual associations (e.g., 'found in gardens') with novel objects influences VOTC representations, such that objects with contextual connections exhibited higher pattern similarity after learning in association with a reduction in pattern information about the object's visual features (Clarke et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Visual imagery triggered by non-visual stimulation is unlikely to explain the processing of auditory information in the VOTC of sighted people.
source: Even if we cannot fully exclude that the processing of auditory information in the VOTC of sighted people could be the by-product of the visual imagery triggered by the non-visual stimulation (Cichy et al., 2012; Kosslyn et al., 1995; Reddy et al., 2010; Slotnick et al., 2005; Stokes et al., 2009), we find it unlikely.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of reasoning including experimental design choices and negative correlation results.

claim: Two separate groups of sighted people were included, each performing the experiment in one modality only, to minimize the influence of having heard or seen the stimuli in the other modality.
source: First, we purposely included two separate groups of sighted people, each one performing the experiment in one modality only, in order to minimize the influence of having heard or seen the stimuli in the other modality in the context of the experiment.
evidence: This is a methodological design choice described in the manuscript.

claim: A fast event-related design was used that restricted the time window to build a visual image of the actual sound.
source: Also, we used a fast event-related design that restricted the time window to build a visual image of the actual sound since the next sound was presented quickly after (Logie, 1989).
evidence: This is a methodological design choice described in the manuscript.

claim: EVC does not discriminate the different sounds in the sighted group.
source: Moreover, we would expect that visual imagery would also triggers information to be processed in posterior occipital regions (Kosslyn et al., 1999). Instead, we found that EVC does not discriminate the different sounds in the sighted group (Figure 3B and Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4A.

claim: The decoding accuracy for the auditory categories in VOTC is significantly higher in the early blind compared to the sighted control group.
source: Interestingly, we found that the decoding accuracy for the auditory categories in VOTC is significantly higher in the early blind compared to the sighted control group (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The correlation between the topographic distribution of categorical response observed in VOTC was stronger in blind versus sighted people.
source: In addition, the correlation between the topographic distribution of categorical response observed in VOTC was stronger in blind versus sighted people (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by topographical selectivity map analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The representational structure of visual categories in sighted was significantly closer to the structure of the auditory categories in blind than in sighted.
source: Moreover, the representational structure of visual categories in sighted was significantly closer to the structure of the auditory categories in blind than in sighted (Figure 4A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4A2.

claim: The representation of the auditory stimuli in VOTC is more similar between blind than between sighted subjects.
source: Finally, the representation of the auditory stimuli in VOTC is more similar between blind than between sighted subjects (Figure 7), showing an increased inter-subject stability of the representation in case of early visual deprivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by inter-subject correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: A categorical organization similar to the one found in vision could emerge in VOTC in absence of visual experience.
source: All together, these results not only demonstrate that a categorical organization similar to the one found in vision could emerge in VOTC in absence of visual experience, but also that such categorical response to sounds is actually enhanced and more stable in congenitally blind people.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing categorical responses in VOTC of blind individuals.

claim: In absence of vision, the occipital cortex enhances its response to non-visual information processing.
source: Several studies have shown that in absence of vision, the occipital cortex enhances its response to non-visual information processing (Collignon et al., 2012; Collignon et al., 2011; Sadato et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The expression of crossmodal plasticity, at least in VOTC, is constrained by the inherent categorical structure endowed in this region.
source: In contrast with this view, our results demonstrate that the expression of crossmodal plasticity, at least in VOTC (see differences in EVC below), is constrained by the inherent categorical structure endowed in this region.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing similar categorical organization across groups.

claim: VOTC reliably encodes sound categories in sighted and blind people using a representational structure and connectivity partially similar to the one found in vision.
source: First, we highlighted remarkably similar functional profile of VOTC for visual and auditory stimuli in sighted and in early blind individuals (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: VOTC is encoding a similar categorical dimension of the stimuli across different inputs of presentation and different visual experiences.
source: In addition, we showed that VOTC is encoding a similar categorical dimension of the stimuli across different inputs of presentation and different visual experiences (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The involvement of right dorsal occipital region for arithmetic processing in blind people relates to the intrinsic 'spatial' nature of these regions.
source: In support of such idea, we recently demonstrated that the involvement of right dorsal occipital region for arithmetic processing in blind people actually relates to the intrinsic 'spatial' nature of these regions, a process involved in specific arithmetic computation (e.g. subtraction but not multiplication) (Crollen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: The involvement of VOTC during 'language' may relate to the fact that some level of representation involved in language (e.g. semantic) can be intrinsically encoded in VOTC.
source: Similarly, the involvement of VOTC during 'language' as observed in previous studies (Bedny et al., 2011; Burton et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2017; Lane et al., 2015; Röder et al., 2002) may relate to the fact that some level of representation involved in language (e.g. semantic) can be intrinsically encoded in VOTC as supported by the current results (Huth et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and inferred from current results.

claim: VOTC regions have innate predispositions relevant to important categorical distinctions that cause category-selective patches to emerge regardless of sensory experience.
source: In fact, we suggest that VOTC regions have innate predispositions relevant to important categorical distinctions that cause category-selective patches to emerge regardless of sensory experience.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Items from a particular broad category (e.g. inanimate) are so diverse that they may not share systematic perceptual features and therefore a higher-level of representation, partially abstracted from vision, might prove important.
source: One argument might be that items from a particular broad category (e.g. inanimate) are so diverse that they may not share systematic perceptual features and therefore a higher-level of representation, partially abstracted from vision, might prove important.
evidence: This is a speculative argument provided to explain the results.

claim: There is evidence in support of an extension of the intrinsic categorical organization of VOTC that is already partially independent from vision in sighted.
source: Indeed, we gather evidence in support of an extension of the intrinsic categorical organization of VOTC that is already partially independent from vision in sighted.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing categorical responses to sounds in sighted individuals.

claim: The crossmodal plasticity observed in early blind individuals may serve to maintain the functional homeostasis of occipital regions.
source: An intriguing possibility raised by our results is that the crossmodal plasticity observed in early blind individuals may actually serve to maintain the functional homeostasis of occipital regions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The specific topographic location of a selective brain function is constrained by an innate profile of functional and structural connections with extrinsic brain regions.
source: It is thought that the specific topographic location of a selective brain functions is constrained by an innate profile of functional and structural connections with extrinsic brain regions (Passingham et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: The main fiber tracts are already present in full-term human neonates.
source: Since the main fiber tracts are already present in full-term human neonates (Dubois et al., 2014; Dubois et al., 2016; Kennedy et al., 1999; Kostović and Judaš, 2010; Marín-Padilla, 2011; Takahashi et al., 2011), such initial connectome may at least partly drive the functional development of a specific area.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The visual word form area (VWFA) in VOTC shows robust and specific anatomical connectivity to EVC and to frontotemporal language networks and this connectivity fingerprint can predict the location of VWFA even before a child learn to read.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the visual word form area (VWFA) in VOTC (McCandliss et al., 2003) shows robust and specific anatomical connectivity to EVC and to frontotemporal language networks and this connectivity fingerprint can predict the location of VWFA even before a child learn to read (Saygin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Anatomical connectivity profile can predict the location of the fusiform face area (FFA).
source: Similarly, anatomical connectivity profile can predict the location of the fusiform face area (FFA) (Saygin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: FFA has a direct structural connection with the temporal voice area (TVA) in the superior temporal sulcus thought to support similar computations applied on faces and voices as well as their integration.
source: In addition to intra-occipital connections, FFA has a direct structural connection with the temporal voice area (TVA) in the superior temporal sulcus (Benetti et al., 2018; Blank et al., 2011) thought to support similar computations applied on faces and voices as well as their integration (von Kriegstein et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The maintenance of selective structural connections between TVA and FFA explains the preferential recruitment of TVA for face processing in congenitally deaf people.
source: Interestingly, recent studies suggested that the maintenance of those selective structural connections between TVA and FFA explains the preferential recruitment of TVA for face processing in congenitally deaf people (Benetti et al., 2018; Benetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The TVA-FFA connectivity may explain why voices preferentially map slightly more lateral to the mid-fusiform sulcus.
source: This TVA-FFA connectivity may explain why voices preferentially map slightly more lateral to the mid-fusiform sulcus (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the connectivity hypothesis and the topographical mapping results.

claim: Sounds of big objects or natural scenes preferentially recruit more mesial VOTC regions, overlapping with the parahippocampal place area, potentially due to the preserved pattern of structural connectivity of those regions in blind people.
source: Similarly, sounds of big objects or natural scenes preferentially recruit more mesial VOTC regions (Figure 1B), overlapping with the parahippocampal place area, potentially due to the preserved pattern of structural connectivity of those regions in blind people (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by topographical mapping results and citation to previous research.

claim: The existence of innate large-scale brain connections specific for each region supporting separate categorical domain may provide the structural scaffolding on which crossmodal inputs capitalize to reach VOTC in both sighted and blind people.
source: The existence of these innate large-scale brain connections that are specific for each region supporting separate categorical domain may provide the structural scaffolding on which crossmodal inputs capitalize to reach VOTC in both sighted and blind people, potentially through feed-back connections.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results.

claim: The main white matter tracks including those involving occipital regions are not significantly different between blind and sighted individuals.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that the main white matter tracks including those involving occipital regions are not significantly different between blind and sighted individuals (Shimony et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In early blind, the absence of competitive visual inputs from feed-forward inputs from EVC may trigger an enhanced weighting of feed-back inter-modal connections leading to an extension of selective categorical response to sounds in VOTC.
source: In EB, the absence of competitive visual inputs typically coming from feed-forward inputs from EVC may actually trigger an enhanced weighting of those feed-back inter-modal connection leading to an extension of selective categorical response to sounds in VOTC, as observed in the current study.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results.

claim: The results provide crucial support for the 'biased connectivity' hypothesis.
source: Our results provide crucial support for this 'biased connectivity' hypothesis (Hannagan et al., 2015; Mahon and Caramazza, 2011) showing that VOTC subregions are part of a large-scale functional network representing categorical information in a format that is at least partially independent from the modality of the stimuli presentation and from the visual experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results and citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Intrinsic characteristics of objects belonging to different categories might drive different representations in the VOTC of the blind.
source: Previous studies already suggested that intrinsic characteristics of objects belonging to different categories might drive different representations in the VOTC of the blind (Bi et al., 2016; Büchel, 2003; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: In the early blind group, the number of voxels selective for animals is reduced compared to the other categories.
source: We found that in the early blind group the number of voxels selective for animals is reduced compared to the other categories (see Figure 2A), suggesting that the animal category is under represented in the VOTC of early blind.
evidence: This claim is supported by voxel count analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The hierarchical clustering analyses highlight a reduced animate/inanimate division in the EBa group, with the animal and the humans categories not clustering together and the animals being represented more like tools or big objects.
source: Our hierarchical clustering analyses (see Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) also highlight a reduced animate/inanimate division in the EBa group, with the animal and the humans categories not clustering together and the animals being represented more like tools or big objects in the EBa.
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Blind people normally learn the peculiar shape of each animal touching static miniature models of them.
source: Blind people, instead, do normally learn the peculiar shape of each animal touching static miniature models of them.
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge about how blind people learn about animals.

claim: When blind people hear the sounds of animals without seeing them, they might combine these sounds with the rest of the environmental sounds.
source: Moreover, when blind people hear the sounds of these animals without seeing them, they might combine these sounds with the rest of the environmental sounds, and this is indeed what we see in the behavioral ratings, in which only blind subjects cluster together animals and big environmental sounds.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral rating results.

claim: The modality of presentation and/or the visual experience do affect the qualitative structure of the categorical representation in VOTC, and this effect is stronger for some categories (i.e. animals) compared to others (i.e. inanimate).
source: These results therefore reveal that the modality of presentation and/or the visual experience do affect the qualitative structure of the categorical representation in VOTC, and this effect is stronger for some categories (i.e. animals) compared to others (i.e. inanimate).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing differences in categorical representation across groups and categories.

claim: Sound categories could be decoded in the EVC of EB but not of the SC.
source: A different profile emerged from EVC. First, sound categories could be decoded in the EVC of EB (Figure 3B) but not of the SC.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The representational structure of EVC for sounds correlated to the one found in vision only in EB.
source: In addition, the representational structure of EVC for sounds correlated to the one found in vision only in EB (Figure 4A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 4A2.

claim: Neither the categorical membership nor the acoustic attributes of sounds correlated with the representational structure found in the EVC of EB.
source: However, neither the categorical membership nor the acoustic attributes of sounds correlated with the representational structure found in the EVC of EB (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The posterior part of the occipital cortex in EB is the region that distances itself the most from the native computation it typically implements.
source: A possible explanation for this result is that the posterior part of the occipital cortex in EB is the region that distances itself the most from the native computation it typically implements (Bi et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents an interpretation of the results.

claim: Because EVC has a native computation that does not easily transfer to another sensory modality (i.e. low-level vision), it may rewire itself for distant functions.
source: Because this area has a native computation that does not easily transfer to another sensory modality (i.e. low-level vision), it may therefore rewire itself for distant functions (Bedny, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Some studies reported an involvement of EVC in high-level linguistic or memory tasks.
source: Some studies, for instance reported an involvement of EVC in high-level linguistic or memory tasks (Van Ackeren et al., 2018; Amedi et al., 2003; Bedny et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The categorical membership of sounds does not explain the representational structure of EVC in the current study.
source: However, as demonstrated here, the categorical membership of sounds, which may be a proxy for semantic representation, does not explain the representational structure of EVC in our study.
evidence: This claim is supported by the representational similarity analysis results.

claim: Early visual deprivation is associated with significant changes in the structure of the brain itself, particularly within the occipital cortex.
source: This is particularly relevant when comparing blind and sighted subjects given that blindness is associated with significant changes in the structure of the brain itself, particularly within the occipital cortex (Dormal et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2009; Pan et al., 2007; Park et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Thirty-four participants completed the auditory version of the fMRI study: 17 early blinds and 17 sighted controls.
source: Thirty-four participants completed the auditory version of the fMRI study: 17 early blinds (EBa; 10F) and 17 sighted controls (SCa; 6F).
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: An additional group of 16 sighted participants performed the visual version of the fMRI experiment.
source: An additional group of 16 sighted participants (SCv; 8F) performed the visual version of the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: All the blind participants lost sight at birth or before 4 years of age and all of them reported not having visual memories and never used vision functionally.
source: All the blind participants lost sight at birth or before 4 years of age and all of them reported not having visual memories and never used vision functionally (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the blind participants' characteristics.

claim: The three groups were age and gender matched.
source: The three groups were age (range 20–67 years, mean ± SD: 33.29 ± 10.24 for EBa subjects, respectively 23–63, 34.12 ± 8.69 for SCa subjects, and 23–51, 30.88 ± 7.24 for SCv subjects) and gender (χ2 (2,50)=1.92, p=0.38) matched.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants and matching procedure.

claim: Sounds and images were used instead of words because the authors wanted to access and model the bottom-up cascade of sensory processing starting from the low-level sensory processing up to the more conceptual level.
source: We decided to use sounds and images, instead of words, because we wanted to access and model the bottom-up cascade of sensory processing starting from the low-level sensory processing up to the more conceptual level.
evidence: This is a methodological decision explained by the authors.

claim: The final acoustic stimulus set included 24 sounds from 8 different categories that could be reduced to 4 superordinate categories.
source: The final acoustic stimulus set included 24 sounds from 8 different categories (human vocalization, human non-vocalization, birds, mammals, tools, graspable objects, environmental scenes, big mechanical objects) that could be reduced to 4 superordinate categories (human, animals, manipulable objects, big objects/places) (see Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus set used in the study.

claim: Binary MVP-classification using SVM classifier was used to distinguish between two categories at a time.
source: We performed a binary MVP-classification (using SVM - support vector machine classifier) to look at the ability of each ROI to distinguish between two categories at time.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method used.

claim: With eight categories, there are 28 possible pairs, resulting in 28 binary MVP-classification tests in each ROI.
source: With eight categories we can have 28 possible pairs, resulting in 28 binary MVP-classification tests in each ROI.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis approach.

claim: Binary MVP-classification was used as dissimilarity index to build neural DSMs.
source: We used the binary MVP-classification as dissimilarity index to build neural DSMs (Carlson et al., 2013; Cichy and Pantazis, 2017; Cichy et al., 2013; Dobs et al., 2019; Haxby et al., 2014; Haxby et al., 2011; O'Toole et al., 2005; Pereira et al., 2009; Proklova et al., 2019) for each group, in order to compare the functional profile of the ROIs between the three groups.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method with citations to previous studies using similar approaches.

claim: Binary MVP-classification was preferred over other dissimilarity measures because two experimental conditions that do not drive a response appear very dissimilar when using correlation-based measures but are indistinguishable when using decoding approaches due to cross-validation.
source: We preferred to use binary MVP-classification as dissimilarity index to build neural DSMs rather than other types of dissimilarity measures (e.g. Pearson correlation, Euclidean distance, Spearman correlation) since two experimental conditions that do not drive a response and therefore have uncorrelated patterns (noise only, r ≈ 0) appear very dissimilar (1 – r ≈ 1). When using a decoding approach instead, due to the intrinsic cross-validation steps, we would find that the two conditions that don't drive responses are indistinguishable, despite their substantial correlation distance (Walther et al., 2016) since the noise is independent between the training and testing partitions, therefore cross-validated estimates of the distance do not grow with increasing noise.
evidence: This is a methodological justification with citation to previous work.

claim: Pitch was selected as the low-level auditory feature because it is distinctly represented in the auditory cortex and may create low-level bias of auditory category selective responses in the temporal cortex.
source: Pitch corresponds to the perceived frequency content of a stimulus. We selected this specific low-level auditory feature for two reasons. First, previous studies showed that this physical property of the sounds is distinctly represented in the auditory cortex and may create some low-level bias of auditory category selective responses in the temporal cortex (Giordano et al., 2013; Leaver and Rauschecker, 2010; Moerel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological justification with citations to previous research.

claim: Among alternative auditory RDMs based on separate acoustic features, the pitch model correlated most with brain RDM extracted from the temporal cortex in the SCa group.
source: Second, we confirmed with our own SCa group that, among alternative auditory RDMs based on separate acoustic features (e.g. Harmonicity on noise ratio, Spectral centroid), the pitch model correlated most with brain RDM extracted from the temporal cortex. This provided strong support that this model was maximally efficient in capturing the encoding of sounds based on acoustic features in auditory cortical regions (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.
